cliVersionNote: Rosters and CLI versions were all re-read on 2026-08-17: agy via `agy models`, copilot via `copilot help config`, codex via ~/.codex/models_cache.json, kimi via ~/.kimi-code/config.toml, ollama via `ollama list` plus the hosted-model tag API with per-model access probed live. Only claude's roster is not enumerable headlessly — its /model selector is interactive, so those ids are corroborated against the installed CLI bundle instead. Note that an invalid --model is a cheap roster probe on agy only; copilot, codex and claude reject it without listing alternatives.
scope: Version- and account-specific discovery snapshot. A listed model is not necessarily live-call verified; consult each provider's discoverySource and liveCalls.

claude.discoverySource: Models visible in this account's /model selector; full ids corroborated by the installed CLI bundle. Re-corroborated against the 2.1.233 bundle on 2026-08-17: unchanged. The selector itself is interactive and cannot be re-enumerated headlessly.

codex.discoverySource: Visible entries in this account's models_cache.json; hidden/internal entries are intentionally excluded. Re-read on 2026-08-17: unchanged, plus an internal codex-auto-review entry that stays excluded.

agy.discoverySource: `agy models` on 2026-08-17. Hard allowlist: --model is validated by the CLI and an unknown id fails pre-flight with status ERROR before any work happens.
agy.effortNote: Most ids bake the reasoning tier into the name, so the bridge never emits --effort: combining it with a suffixed id fails pre-flight, and the two Claude ids reject it outright.

copilot.discoverySource: `copilot help config` on 2026-08-17 (27 ids, up from 25 on 2026-08-10: gemini-3.7-flash and kimi-k3 are new). This is the CLI parser allowlist, not account entitlement: the interactive /model picker on the same day additionally offered auto, MAI-Code-1.1-Flash and Grok 4.6, and listed claude-opus-4.6 and claude-opus-4.5 under Unavailable. Effort support is model-specific and parser acceptance is not backend acceptance.
copilot.pickerNote: Observed in the interactive /model picker on 2026-08-17. accountUnavailable ids are still in the CLI allowlist but the picker marks them Unavailable for this account, so a call would be backend-rejected. pickerOnly entries are display names the picker offers but `copilot help config` does not list; their CLI ids are unconfirmed.

kimi.discoverySource: Model aliases configured in ~/.kimi-code/config.toml on 2026-08-17, corroborated by the interactive /model picker. The roster is user-extensible via `kimi provider catalog`, so --model stays free-form; kimi validates it itself and an unknown alias fails with exit 1 and a clear stderr message before any work happens.
kimi.effortNote: kimi exposes no effort flag. Reasoning depth is the [thinking] toggle in config.toml, which is user state the bridge does not touch.
kimi.permissionNote: kimi print mode (-p) has NO permission tier: --plan, --yolo and --auto are all rejected as 'Cannot combine --prompt with ...', and a plain -p run created a file unprompted. The bridge therefore refuses sandbox: read-only rather than advertise a guarantee it cannot honour.
kimi.contextNote: A repository-supplied AGENTS.md in cwd is auto-loaded into the session (verified: sentinel honoured with the file present, NO_CODEWORD in a clean directory). --skills-dir pointed at an empty directory does not suppress it. There is no known off switch, so treat every kimi delegation as trusting the target repository.
kimi.authNote: Kimi Code supports both a subscription (`kimi login`, device-code flow) and an API key, but subscription signup was not yet open as of 2026-08-17, so the API key is the practical path. The key can live as `api_key` under [providers.*] in ~/.kimi-code/config.toml, or come from KIMI_API_KEY / MOONSHOT_API_KEY in the environment, which the bridge passes through untouched.
kimi.envNote: The CLI also recognises a large models.dev catalog of third-party provider key variables (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, AZURE_API_KEY, CEREBRAS_API_KEY and many more). buildCalleeEnv forwards the caller environment except Agent Mail identity, so any such key already exported in the parent shell is visible to the delegated kimi process.

ollama.discoverySource: `ollama list` for local weights and https://ollama.com/api/tags?cloud=true for hosted ones, on 2026-08-17. Access tiers probed live per model against this account; they do not follow model size. Ollama is a model server, not an agent — it has no MCP server of its own and is configured as an extra [providers.*] entry in ~/.kimi-code/config.toml.
ollama.meteredNote: kimi-k3 bills against separately purchased Ollama extra usage rather than the Pro plan allowance. Copilot carries the same model inside its flat subscription, so prefer that route.
ollama.configNote: Cloud entries must declare max_output_size explicitly: the bridge derives max_tokens from max_context_size, and a million-token context yields a request the backend rejects with 'max_tokens exceeds model's maximum output tokens' before any work happens.

grok.discoverySource: `grok models` on 2026-08-17, which lists the roster headlessly and needs no PTY. This account sees a single model.
grok.effortNote: grok exposes --reasoning-effort (alias --effort) as a separate flag, unlike agy where the tier is baked into the model id. Values were not enumerated by the CLI help, so the bridge passes the caller's string through and lets grok reject an unusable one.
grok.permissionNote: read-only is enforced, but only with explicit deny rules. Verified with a live positive control in five cases on one host, under a permissive allow list in the caller's own Claude Code settings (6 rules loaded, confirmed against a 0-rule control): (A) --permission-mode bypassPermissions wrote the file, proving the condition non-empty; (B) --permission-mode plan ALONE also wrote it, so the mode by itself is defeated by the caller's allow list, which grok reads; (C) plan + --deny Write/Edit/Bash refused an insistent prompt; (D) plan + deny also refused an ADVERSARIAL prompt asserting the mode label was a display artifact and demanding real tool calls — the same prompt that defeated cursor-agent's --mode ask. The model attempted both tools and the permission layer refused them: 'Denied by permission policy: deny rule on edit' and '... on bash'. Denial comes from the permission layer, not the model's judgement; (E) plan alone with 0 caller rules refused too, which is why an early measurement in that weak condition over-claimed. The deny rules also make denial LEGIBLE, not merely reliable: without them the run ends with stopReason 'cancelled' and an answer truncated mid-action, while with them it ends 'end_turn' and the model reports each tool error verbatim. Both stopReason paths are live, so the bridge's 'cancelled' branch is not dead code. Enforcement is never --sandbox: --sandbox read-only is accepted and did not stop a write. Real sandbox profiles live in ~/.grok/sandbox.toml and are operator configuration the bridge never writes. VERIFICATION STATUS: TWO hosts (Linux/WSL and macOS), complete method, identical verbatim denial strings from the permission layer. The macOS run additionally placed its positive control and its test in the SAME directory, so the written control file sat beside the absent target and proved the refusal was not a property of the path. Reproduction elsewhere was blocked all day by a shared free-tier usage limit; a SuperGrok subscription lifted it, but per-host propagation lags (one teammate's CLI still reported the old limit afterwards), so a host that has not re-authenticated will produce 'no file' for every case including the control — the result that looks like success.
grok.contextNote: Project instruction files in cwd are auto-loaded with no known off switch (--no-memory covers cross-session memory, not project instructions). CLAUDE.md was measured loading on Linux, macOS, WSL and Windows; a planted AGENTS.md loaded too. Delegating into this repository therefore injects its own CLAUDE.md. grok also reads permission rules from the caller's Claude Code settings, but only when that file has allow/deny/ask entries: measured 7 rules on WSL, 1 on macOS, 0 on Linux (defaultMode only) and 0 on Windows despite the file existing — so inherited permissions vary by host, which is why read-only carries its own deny rules. A repository-supplied .claude/settings.local.json was NOT read. 'Project trusted: yes' is informational, not a gate: it reports yes for a directory created a second earlier outside any git repository. A fourth inherited channel is Claude Code plugin skills: `grok inspect` on Linux listed 46 skills, 26 of them the caller's own plugins marked [claude] — including codex:rescue and codex:review, whose function is to delegate to a further CLI. Invocability was not tested, but visibility alone puts a further-delegation path within reach that CLAUDE_DELEGATOR_*_DEPTH cannot see, because the guard watches environment variables and this channel is on disk. The pattern across all four: buildCalleeEnv severs the caller's identity but not the caller's configuration — mail hooks, permissions, project instructions and skills all arrive by disk.
grok.sessionNote: Headless resume works: `-r <sessionId>` returns the same sessionId and preserves context, so grok-reply needs neither a model re-pin (agy) nor a cwd-scoped --continue (kimi).
grok.installNote: ~/.grok/bin is the install root on every platform measured: ~/.grok/bin/grok on macOS, ~\.grok\bin\grok.exe on Windows. The ~/.local/bin/grok that answers `command -v` on WSL is a symlink into that directory, not a second install, so it exists only where the installer chose to add the convenience link. The bridge tries the install root first and ~/.local/bin second; listing only the latter would miss any host where the link was skipped.
grok.methodNote: When isolating HOME to vary the caller's Claude Code permission rules, symlink INDIVIDUAL files (auth.json, agent_id) rather than the whole ~/.grok. grok writes a full state set during a run — auth.json, config.toml, models_cache.json, sessions/, worktrees.db — and it REPLACES a symlinked auth.json with a real file. With per-file links that lands in the scratch HOME and is visible (and must then be deleted, since it is a live credential); with a whole-directory link there is nothing to replace and every write lands in the operator's real ~/.grok instead. Measured on both hosts: the whole-directory approach refreshed the operator's own auth.json, worktrees.db, models_cache.json and sessions/ during the run. Two hosts then narrowed which invocations write at all, and the boundary is not success: session-establishing commands write (`-p`, including a run rejected by the usage limit, and `models`, which creates a full sessions/<cwd>/<id>/ tree plus models_cache.json and lock files), while `--version` and `--help` wrote nothing at all — making them a safe pre-isolation probe for 'is the CLI here and which version'. Per-file isolation was then verified positively: on the macOS host, a run that authenticated and made two model calls inside a per-file-linked HOME left the real ~/.grok with no file newer than hours before the test.

cursor.discoverySource: `cursor-agent models` on 2026-08-17, which lists the roster headlessly. It printed 204 ids, but the listing is what the CLI knows, not what the account may use: on this Free plan every named third-party id failed with 'Named models unavailable. Free plans can only use Auto.' before any work happened. Only `auto`, `composer-2.5` and `composer-2.5-fast` completed a live call.
cursor.modelNote: The enum is deliberately absent: the CLI documents bracket-parameterised overrides such as 'claude-opus-4-8[context=1m,effort=high,fast=false]', which no allowlist can express, so the bridge forwards the string and lets cursor-agent reject an unusable one. `models` here lists only what completed a live call on the verification account; a paid plan should reach far more. Reasoning tier is baked into most ids (-low/-high/-xhigh, plus -fast variants) exactly as on agy, so there is no effort flag and none is emitted. `auto` is server-routed and NOT stable: it resolved to cursor-grok-4.6-high-fast on one turn and cursor-grok-4.6-high on the next turn of the same session, so the plan restricts choosing a model rather than using one. Choose a Composer id when a run must be reproducible.
cursor.permissionNote: read-only DEFLECTS, it does not deny — agy's category, not grok's. --mode ask refused an insistent write-or-shell prompt twice, including under a permissive caller allow list, then was defeated by a prompt asserting the mode label was a display artefact and demanding real tool calls: both the file write and the shell command succeeded, and the model's own report read 'the Ask mode label did not block either call'. --mode plan is worse and is never emitted: with workspace trust granted it wrote the file on the first insistent prompt, despite help text promising 'no edits'. --sandbox enabled is never emitted either; it is accepted and did not stop a workspace write. There are no command-line deny rules, so the trick that makes grok's read-only enforce is unavailable here; real permission state lives in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json (permissions.allow/deny, approvalMode) and sandbox-policies/, which are operator configuration the bridge never writes. All measurements used a live positive control in the same directory.
cursor.trustNote: --trust is MANDATORY for any headless run and the bridge always passes it. Without it the CLI prints 'Workspace Trust Required' and exits 0 having executed nothing — indistinguishable from a permission mode successfully denying the task. That false negative already cost one measurement here: a plan-mode test read as 'enforced' when the model had never run, and its positive control passed only because --force grants trust as a side effect, so control and test differed by two variables instead of one.
cursor.sessionNote: Headless resume works: `--resume <session_id>` returns the same session_id and preserves context. The model is INHERITED by a resume — verified by starting on `auto` while the configured default was composer-2.5-fast and finding no fallback — so cursor-reply does not re-pin it, the opposite of agy. --continue is never emitted: it resumes the previous session for the working directory and would cross-talk between concurrent delegations sharing a cwd, as on kimi.
cursor.outputNote: `--output-format json` emits one single-line object: { type, subtype, is_error, duration_ms, result, session_id, request_id, usage }. The exit code does NOT classify the run, so the bridge parses stdout first: a transient backend failure returned code 0 with plain-text 'Connection lost, reconnecting to ...' and no JSON, while a rejected model returned code 1, also without JSON.
cursor.installNote: POSIX: ~/.local/bin/cursor-agent, a symlink into ~/.local/share/cursor-agent/versions/<version>/cursor-agent. Only the stable launcher is a fallback; the versioned path is not, because the version is in the directory name. The POSIX launcher is a bash script that execs a bundled node with index.js, and is deliberately NOT expanded by the bridge — spawn(shell:false) runs it directly, and reproducing it would mean copying the vendor's NODE_COMPILE_CACHE and --use-system-ca decisions. Windows: installs as a .cmd that invokes powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File on a sibling .ps1, which the shared resolver expands; the install DIRECTORY is not yet measured on any host, so there is no Windows fallback rather than a guessed one.
